blocks.text: The account does not move directly from Saul’s encounter to public preaching. He is unable to see, must be led into Damascus, fasts for three days, and receives Ananias’s touch, baptism, food, and fellowship before entering his mission. The sequence keeps dependency and care within the call narrative; it does not require readers to identify this temporary blindness with every later hardship associated with Paul.

Acts tells Saul’s call and his early Jerusalem contacts as part of a continuous later narrative, while Galatians offers a selective first-person account with its own purposes and intervals. Their differing selection, emphasis, and sequence make exact harmonization disputed. A careful comparison therefore avoids both treating Acts as a verbatim transcript and assuming that every difference is a contradiction.

Paul’s appearance claim in 1 Corinthians 15 belongs to a death-burial-resurrection-appearance sequence that culminates in Paul himself. That letter should remain distinct from Acts’ later narrative of the Damascus encounter rather than being made to supply details Acts does not give.

Tabitha is explicitly called a disciple, and the widows’ display of the garments she made shows the concrete shape of her good works. Her presence fits Acts’ wider, though selective, portrayal of women as active disciples and workers within the movement.

Acts survives in early papyri and major Greek codices, including P45, P53, P74, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae. These witnesses preserve differing portions and textual profiles; Bezae in particular represents a substantially distinctive form of Acts whose individual readings need case-by-case assessment. More broadly, historical judgments about Acts are best made claim by claim through comparison with independent evidence, rather than by assigning the whole book blanket reliability or unreliability.
